questions.q: At a debate, Arjun argues: 'The Vedic hymns praise Indra, Agni, Varuna and many other deities, so the early seers must have believed in many separate, competing powers.' Which line from the chapter best answers him?
questions.a: 'The Existent is one, but sages give it many names' shows that the early rishis and rishikas saw the many deities as one, not as separate beings. The other lines are real lines from the chapter but speak of unity among people, the wish for all creatures' happiness and the Upanishadic oneness of the Self.
o: 'The Existent is one, but sages give it many names.'
'Come together, speak together; common be your mind.'
'May all creatures be happy', free from disease and sorrow.
'You are That', said Uddalaka to his son Shvetaketu.

questions.q: The chapter says the Vedas were passed on for 'anything between 100 and 200 generations'. Ravi concludes that experts know the exact number of generations but disagree about how long a generation is. Which reading of the phrase fits the way the chapter introduces it?
questions.a: The sentence just before it says experts have proposed dates for the Rig Veda from the 5th to the 2nd millennium BCE, and the next sentence begins 'So, for anything between 100 and 200 generations'. The range comes with an uncertain date, not with an exact count of generations, so Ravi's reading does not fit. UNESCO is mentioned only after the phrase, and the phrase counts generations, not hymns or composers.
o: It is given, with 'So', right after the wide span of dates proposed for the Rig Veda
It is given right after UNESCO's count of chanters, recorded in 2008
It is given as 100 hymns, each of them passed on for 200 years
It is given right after a count of the rishis and rishikas who first composed the hymns of the Rig Veda

questions.q: Tanvi writes: 'Ritam in the Vedas and brahman in the Upanishads are two names for the same idea, since both are about the whole cosmos.' Which difference drawn from the chapter shows her mistake?
questions.a: The chapter says the Vedic deities, together with the seers, sustained ritam, truth and order in human life and in the cosmos; the Upanishadic school of Vedanta says everything is one divine essence called brahman. One is an order that is kept up, the other is what everything is. The swapped pair reverses them, offerings to Agni are yajna, brahman is not the god Brahma, and the Self in each being is the atman.
o: Ritam is truth and order the deities and seers sustained; brahman is the one essence everything is
Ritam is the one essence that everything is; brahman is the truth and order the deities and seers sustained
Ritam is a daily offering made to Agni; brahman is the god Brahma whom the seers praised
Ritam is the Self living in each being; brahman is the order kept in the sky and the seasons

questions.q: A tour guide at a museum tells visitors: 'The Vedic hymns were composed in Pali by monks.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The hymns were composed in an early form of Sanskrit by rishis (male seers) and rishikas (female seers). Bhikshus and bhikshunis are the Buddhist monks and nuns of the Sangha, and rajas were rulers of the janas, not composers of hymns.
o: In early Sanskrit, by rishis and rishikas
In early Sanskrit, by bhikshus and bhikshunis
In a form of Hindi, by rishis and rishikas
In early Sanskrit, by the rajas of the janas

questions.q: Taking one generation as 25 years, the lower figure the chapter gives for the oral passing-on of the Vedas works out to about ___ years.

Match each description in Column A with the term from the chapter in Column B.
Column A: 1. The root shared by the words 'Veda' and 'vidya'  2. A verse, such as the last ones of the Rig Veda that call for unity  3. The way the hymns crossed 100 to 200 generations  4. The world seen as an ordered and harmonious system
Column B: a. cosmos  b. mantra  c. vid  d. memorised recitation
questions.a: 1-c (vid means knowledge), 2-b (mantras are verses), 3-d (the hymns were committed to memory and passed on orally), 4-a (the chapter's meaning of cosmos).

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Vedas.
1. Of the four Vedas, the Rig Veda is the most ancient.
2. The Vedic hymns were addressed to the deities in the form of prose instructions.
3. Experts have proposed dates for the Rig Veda ranging from the 5th to the 2nd millennium BCE.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are what the chapter says. Statement 2 is false: the hymns were prayers in the form of poems and songs, addressed to the deities in poetical form.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In 2008, UNESCO recognised Vedic chanting as a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity.
Reason (R): For 100 to 200 generations the Vedic texts were memorised through rigorous training and passed on orally with hardly any alterations.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and the chapter itself says this meticulous transmission over thousands of years explains why UNESCO gave the recognition, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Meena says, 'Anything that is never written down changes a little every time it is passed on, like a rumour.' (a) What does the chapter say about the Vedas that goes against her rule? (b) What does the chapter say made the difference?
questions.a: (a) The Vedas were passed on orally for 100 to 200 generations with hardly any alterations. (b) They were committed to memory through rigorous training, a meticulous way of passing them on.
s: Part (a): passed on orally for 100-200 generations with hardly any change
Part (b): rigorous training in memorising them

questions.q: The chapter opens with a saying that calls true knowledge 'that which cannot be stolen'. (a) A classmate says the word 'Veda' comes from a word meaning 'song', because the hymns were sung. Correct her, and name one other word the chapter says comes from the same root. (b) Using your answer to (a), explain why a body of knowledge kept only in trained memory fits the line 'that which cannot be stolen'.
questions.a: (a) 'Veda' comes from the Sanskrit vid, meaning 'knowledge', not 'song'; vidya comes from the same root. (b) The Vedas are knowledge, and that knowledge was recited and memorised, not written on an object, so there was no book that a thief or a ruler could take away; it lived in the people who carried it.
s: Part (a): vid means knowledge, not song; vidya shares the root
Part (b): knowledge held in memory, not on an object, so nothing could be taken away

questions.q: True or False? 'Although the Vedas are counted among India's texts, the chapter also gives them as an example of an oral tradition.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. When the chapter defines oral traditions as teachings or practices passed on without written texts, it adds that this is the case of the Vedas: they are called texts, but their hymns were recited and memorised, not written.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the chapter says oral traditions without written texts include the Vedas, whose hymns were recited, not written

questions.q: A newspaper headline reads: 'UNESCO declares the Vedic books a world heritage in 2008.' (a) State exactly what the chapter says UNESCO recognised. (b) Why does the word 'books' in the headline miss the point of that recognition?
questions.a: (a) Vedic chanting, as a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity. (b) What was recognised was the chanting itself, carried by memory and recitation over thousands of years, not a written book.
s: Part (a): Vedic chanting as a masterpiece of oral and intangible heritage
Part (b): the heritage is the oral chanting, not a written object

questions.q: A student's chart is titled 'The five Vedas' and lists the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva Veda and the Upanishads. (a) What is wrong with the chart? (b) How does the chapter describe the Upanishads instead?
questions.a: (a) There are four Vedas; the Upanishads are not a fifth Veda. (b) The Upanishads are a group of texts that built upon Vedic concepts and introduced new ones, such as rebirth and karma.
s: Part (a): only four Vedas; the Upanishads are not one of them
Part (b): a group of texts that built on Vedic ideas and added new ones

questions.q: Kabir writes in his project: 'The Vedas are the oldest texts of India and the oldest texts in the whole world.' Is he right? Test each half of his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is supported: the chapter calls the Vedas the most ancient texts of India. The second half goes too far: the chapter says they are 'among the most ancient in the world', not the oldest of all, so he should write 'among the oldest in the world'.
s: Verdict: partly right
First half supported: the most ancient texts of India
Second half corrected: among the most ancient in the world, not the oldest

questions.q: Show, using the chapter, that the Rig Veda cannot have been composed after the time of the Buddha.
questions.a: The latest date experts propose for the Rig Veda is the 2nd millennium BCE, while Siddhartha Gautama was born about two-and-a-half millenniums ago. The chapter also says Buddhism did not accept the authority of the Vedas, which means the Vedas already existed and had authority when Buddhism arose. So the Rig Veda came first.
s: Latest proposed date for the Rig Veda (2nd millennium BCE) is before the Buddha's birth about 2,500 years ago
Buddhism rejected the Vedas' authority, so the Vedas already existed
Conclusion that the Rig Veda came before the Buddha

questions.q: Write a short scene of four or five lines between a teacher and a pupil in Vedic times that shows how a hymn reached the next generation. Your scene must bring in three facts from the chapter.
questions.a: Any scene that correctly uses three facts, for example: the teacher recites a hymn to Ushas or Agni in an early form of Sanskrit; the pupil repeats it until it is word-perfect (rigorous training, no writing); the teacher says it was composed by a rishi or rishika long ago and must be passed on without change, as it has been for generations.
s: Shows the hymn being recited and memorised, not written
Uses a second correct fact (language, a named deity, or rishis and rishikas)
Uses a third correct fact (passing on without alteration across generations)

questions.q: A website says: 'The Vedas are one written rulebook, composed only by men, praising many separate gods, and they were forgotten for centuries before being rediscovered.' Evaluate the website's statement, testing each of its claims against the chapter.
questions.a: Not one rulebook: there are four Vedas made of thousands of hymns, prayers in the form of poems and songs. Not written: they were recited orally and memorised. Not only men: hymns were composed by rishis and also rishikas, female seers. Not separate gods: the early seers saw the deities as one, 'the Existent is one, but sages give it many names'. Not forgotten: they were passed on for 100 to 200 generations with hardly any change, and UNESCO recognised Vedic chanting in 2008. Verdict: the statement is wrong on every count.
s: Four Vedas of hymns, not one rulebook
Oral and memorised, not written
Rishikas as well as rishis composed hymns
The deities were seen as one truth with many names
Continuous oral passing-on over 100-200 generations, not forgotten

questions.q:
For a wall chart on the Vedic worldview, five lines have been cut out:
Line 1: 'Together with the seers, the deities sustained truth and order in human life and in the cosmos.'
Line 2: 'The Existent is one, but sages give it many names.'
Line 3: 'Come together, speak together; common be your mind.'
Line 4: 'Truth was often another name for God.'
Line 5: 'May your thoughts be united, so all may agree!'
The chart has four headings: (A) the many deities seen as one, (B) ritam, (C) a value placed first, (D) unity among people. Place each line under one heading, and for each line write one sentence on what it shows about the Vedic worldview. Which heading gets two lines, and where in the Rig Veda does the chapter say those lines come from?
questions.a: Line 1 under (B): ritam is the truth and order that the deities and seers kept up together, so the deities stood for order, not only power. Line 2 under (A): the early rishis and rishikas saw the deities as one reality given many names. Line 3 under (D): people are asked to speak and think together. Line 4 under (C): Truth was especially important, often another name for God. Line 5 under (D) as well: it asks that all agree. Heading (D) gets two lines; the chapter says they come from the last mantras of the Rig Veda, which call for unity among people.
s: Line 1 placed under ritam, with what it shows
Line 2 placed under the deities seen as one, with what it shows
Line 4 placed under the value of Truth, with what it shows
Lines 3 and 5 both placed under unity among people
Unity heading gets two lines, from the last mantras of the Rig Veda

questions.q:
Class 6B is preparing a two-minute radio script for a 2026 school broadcast. Their draft reads:
'In ____, UNESCO recognised Vedic chanting as a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity. Our hymns crossed between ____ and ____ generations without being written down. We close with a verse for our theme, "Let us think together and agree".'
The two verses they are choosing between are: Verse X, 'The Existent is one, but sages give it many names'; Verse Y, 'Come together, speak together; common be your mind'.
(a) Fill the first blank and say how many years before the broadcast the recognition came.
(b) Fill the next two blanks and convert them into years, taking one generation as 30 years.
(c) Which verse should close the broadcast? Justify the choice from what each verse is about.
questions.a: (a) 2008; 2026 - 2008 = 18 years before. (b) 100 and 200 generations; 100 x 30 = 3,000 years and 200 x 30 = 6,000 years. (c) Verse Y. It comes from the last mantras of the Rig Veda, which call on people to come together, think alike and agree, which is the class's theme. Verse X is about the many deities being one reality given many names; it says nothing about people thinking together.
s: Part (a): 2008 and 18 years
Part (b): 100 and 200 generations, 3,000 to 6,000 years
Part (c): Verse Y, because it calls for unity among people while Verse X is about the deities being one

questions.q:
In an inter-house quiz on the Vedas, each right answer earns 3 points and each wrong answer loses 1 point. Agni House wrote:
Q1 Meaning of 'vid': song
Q2 Number of Vedas: four
Q3 Composers of the hymns: rishis and rishikas
Q4 How the hymns were passed on: copied on leaves by scribes
Q5 Year of UNESCO's recognition: 2008
Q6 Most ancient of the Vedas: Sama Veda
The rival house has finished with 10 points.
(a) Which of Agni House's answers are wrong?
(b) Give the chapter's correct answer for each wrong one.
(c) What is Agni House's score?
(d) The quizmaster lets Agni House correct one answer only. Can it now beat the rival house? Show the working.
questions.a: (a) Q1, Q4 and Q6. (b) Q1 knowledge; Q4 recited orally and memorised; Q6 the Rig Veda. (c) 3 right, 3 wrong: 3 x 3 - 3 = 6 points. (d) No. With one correction it has 4 right and 2 wrong: 12 - 2 = 10, which only ties with 10. It would need two corrections (5 right, 1 wrong = 14) to win.
s: Part (a): Q1, Q4 and Q6 are wrong
Part (b): knowledge, oral memorised recitation, the Rig Veda
Part (c): 9 - 3 = 6 points
Part (d): no, one correction gives 10 and only ties

questions.q: (a) What does the word 'jana' mean in the chapter? (b) The chapter says ancient India had no separate word for 'tribe'. How does it use the idea of a jana to describe tribes instead?
questions.a: (a) A clan, that is, a larger group of people. (b) Tribes were simply different janas that lived in a specific environment, such as forests or mountains.
s: Part (a): a clan or larger group of people
Part (b): tribes were janas living in a particular environment such as forests or mountains

questions.q:
For a class display, a teacher hands out twelve word cards, each taken from what the chapter says about early Vedic society: raja, sabha, samiti, Bharatas, Purus, Kurus, Yadus, Turvashas, potter, weaver, healer, barber. Pupils must sort them into three groups and then write one line on which group tells the least certain story.
(a) Sort the cards into janas, clues to governance and professions, and give the number in each group.
(b) Among the governance cards, how many point to a gathering of people rather than to one ruler?
(c) Which group tells historians the least certain story? Justify your choice from what the chapter says.
questions.a: (a) Janas: Bharatas, Purus, Kurus, Yadus, Turvashas (5). Governance: raja, sabha, samiti (3). Professions: potter, weaver, healer, barber (4). (b) Two, sabha and samiti, which both mean a collective gathering or assembly; raja means a king or ruler. (c) The governance group. The chapter says not much is known of how the janas governed their society and that the Vedas give only a few clues through these words, while the janas and the professions are named directly in the texts.
s: Part (a): 5 janas, 3 governance words, 4 professions
Part (b): two, sabha and samiti
Part (c): governance, because the chapter says little is known and the words are only clues

questions.q: A historian reads a Vedic hymn that mentions a samiti. Going by the chapter, which conclusion is the safest one to draw?
questions.a: The chapter says sabha and samiti both refer to a collective gathering or assembly, and that the words are only clues. It does not say anything about yearly elections or a palace, and samiti is not one of the professions it lists.
o: The jana's people sometimes met together
The jana elected its raja by vote every year
The samiti was the name of the raja's palace
A samiti was a craftsman, like a potter

questions.q:
Read the statements about early Vedic society.
1. The Vedas give a detailed account of how the janas governed their society.
2. The words sabha and samiti both refer to a collective gathering or assembly.
3. The Rig Veda lists exactly five janas: the Bharatas, Purus, Kurus, Yadus and Turvashas.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 2 is correct. Statement 1 is false because the chapter says not much is known and the Vedas give only a few clues. Statement 3 is false because the Rig Veda alone lists over 30 janas; the five are only examples.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Ira claims: 'Each jana was linked to a region of the northwest, so the janas were really the same thing as today's States, each with its own government.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. A jana was a clan, a larger group of people, so it was a group of people and not a territory with fixed borders like a State. The chapter only says each clan was associated with a particular region. It also says not much is known about how the janas governed themselves, apart from clues such as raja, sabha and samiti, so we cannot claim they had governments like a State.
s: Verdict: disagree
A jana was a clan of people, only associated with a region
Little is known of jana governance, only a few clue-words, so the comparison cannot be supported

questions.q: The chapter says ancient India had no word for 'tribe': tribes were janas that lived in a specific environment such as forests or mountains. From this a pupil concludes that the Bharatas and the Kurus must have been forest tribes. Which point shows the flaw in her reasoning?
questions.a: Tribes were a kind of jana (janas living in a specific environment), but that does not make every jana a tribe. The Rig Veda's janas, such as the Bharatas and Kurus, are described only as clans each associated with a region of the northwest; no forest or mountain setting is given. They are janas, not professions; ancient India had no word for tribe; and the chapter links them to the northwest, not the south.
o: Every tribe was a jana, but the chapter does not say every jana lived in forests
The Bharatas and the Kurus were professions like weaving, not janas
Ancient India had a separate word for tribe, never used for the Kurus
The chapter places the Bharatas and the Kurus in the far south, away from forests

questions.q: If the Rig Veda's list of janas held exactly the round number the chapter quotes, then the janas the chapter names one by one would make up 1 in every ___ janas of that list.
True or False? 'Although each jana had its own region, all five janas the chapter names belonged to the same part of the Subcontinent.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The chapter says each clan was associated with a particular region of the northwest part of the Subcontinent, so the Bharatas, Purus, Kurus, Yadus and Turvashas each had a region of their own, but all of those regions lay in the northwest.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: each clan had its own region, but every one was in the northwest part of the Subcontinent

questions.q:
A children's magazine plans a two-page spread called 'Life in a Vedic Jana' with four panels:
Panel 1: 'The Kurus, one of the janas of the south of the Subcontinent'
Panel 2: 'The raja and the parliament elected by every citizen'
Panel 3: 'Weavers, potters, carpenters and healers'
Panel 4: 'The Rig Veda names over 300 janas'
Evaluate each panel against the chapter, rewrite every panel that is wrong, and suggest one more panel that the chapter does support.
questions.a: Panel 1 is wrong: the Kurus are a jana, but each clan was associated with a region of the northwest, so it should read 'The Kurus, one of the janas of the northwest'. Panel 2 goes beyond the chapter: it gives only the clue-words raja, sabha and samiti, with sabha and samiti meaning a gathering or assembly, and says not much is known of how janas governed; it should read 'The raja, the sabha and the samiti: clues to how janas were run'. Panel 3 is supported by the chapter's list of professions. Panel 4 is wrong by a factor of ten: the Rig Veda alone lists over 30 janas. A fifth panel could show other professions, such as builder, dancer, barber, agriculturist or priest, or the Bharatas, Purus, Yadus and Turvashas.
s: Panel 1 corrected: a jana of the northwest, not the south
Panel 2 corrected: only clue-words raja, sabha, samiti; little known
Panel 3 judged supported by the professions list
Panel 4 corrected: over 30 janas, not 300
A fifth panel that the chapter supports

questions.q:
Match each scene from a Vedic village in Column A with the word from the chapter in Column B.
Column A: 1. A large group of related families such as the Purus  2. The people of the clan meet together to talk  3. One person rules the clan  4. A woman treats a fever using traditional practices
Column B: a. healer  b. raja  c. sabha  d. jana
questions.a: 1-d (a jana is a clan, a larger group of people), 2-c (a sabha is a collective gathering), 3-b (a raja is a king or ruler), 4-a (a healer uses traditional practices to relieve or heal diseases).

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Historians can say only a little about how the early Vedic janas governed their society.
Reason (R): The Vedic texts mention many professions, such as weaver, potter, carpenter and healer.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. A is true because the Vedas give only a few clues, such as raja, sabha and samiti. R is also true, but a list of professions tells us about work, not about how the janas were governed, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Rohan says, 'The Vedas are hymns to deities, so they tell us nothing about the ordinary people of the time.' (a) Give one piece of evidence from the chapter that the Vedic texts do tell us about ordinary people's lives. (b) Give a second, different kind of evidence.
questions.a: (a) The Vedic texts mention many professions, such as agriculturist, weaver, potter, builder, carpenter, healer, dancer, barber and priest. (b) The Rig Veda names over 30 janas, the clans people lived in, such as the Bharatas, Purus and Kurus, each linked to a region of the northwest; or the words raja, sabha and samiti give clues to how people were governed.
s: Part (a): the professions the Vedas mention
Part (b): a different kind of evidence, the named janas or the governance clue-words

questions.q:
A school team is building a model of an early Vedic village with a budget of Rs 1,500. Their plan and prices: a raja figure Rs 150; a potter, a weaver and a carpenter figure at Rs 90 each; a royal palace with a throne room Rs 400; a samiti scene (labelled 'samiti') Rs 350. Extra items the shop sells: a second assembly scene labelled 'sabha' Rs 350, and more profession figures at Rs 90 each. The teacher's rule: the model may show only what the chapter supports.
(a) Which planned item does the chapter give no support for? Say why.
(b) What do the supported planned items cost together?
(c) How much money is left after buying only the supported items?
(d) The team wants the model to carry a label for every governance clue-word the chapter gives, and also two more profession figures. Which extra item must it buy, and can it afford all of this? Show the working.
questions.a: (a) The royal palace with a throne room: the chapter says not much is known of how the janas governed and gives only the words raja, sabha and samiti, with nothing about palaces. (b) 150 + 3 x 90 + 350 = Rs 770. (c) 1,500 - 770 = Rs 730. (d) The clue-words are raja, sabha and samiti; raja and samiti are already there, so it must buy the sabha scene (Rs 350). 350 + 2 x 90 = Rs 530, which is less than Rs 730, so it can afford it and will have Rs 200 left.
s: Part (a): the palace, because the chapter gives only clue-words about governance
Part (b): Rs 770
Part (c): Rs 730
Part (d): buy the sabha scene; Rs 530 fits, Rs 200 left

questions.q: Pupils sort words found in the Vedic texts into 'clues to governance' and 'professions'. Which sorting is fully correct?
questions.a: Raja (ruler), sabha and samiti (gatherings) are the chapter's clues to governance; potter, healer and barber are among the professions it lists. Each wrong sorting moves a gathering word into the professions or a profession into governance.
o: Governance: raja, sabha, samiti | Professions: potter, healer, barber
Governance: raja, priest, samiti | Professions: potter, sabha, barber
Governance: raja, sabha | Professions: samiti, healer, potter, barber
Governance: sabha, samiti, healer | Professions: raja, potter, barber

questions.q: Write three sentences that a person living in an early Vedic jana might say about her own day. Sentence 1 must use the name of a jana, sentence 2 a governance clue-word, and sentence 3 a profession, each used the way the chapter uses it. Then say which of your three sentences a historian could least rely on, and why.
questions.a: Any three fitting sentences, for example: 'I belong to the Purus, whose land is in the northwest.' 'Today the people of our clan meet in the sabha.' 'My brother is a potter.' The sentence a historian could least rely on is the governance one: the chapter says the words raja, sabha and samiti are only a few clues and not much is known of how the janas governed, so what happened at a sabha is guesswork.
s: Sentence using a named jana (with the northwest, if a place is given)
Sentences using a governance clue-word and a profession correctly
Names the governance sentence as least reliable, because the words are only clues

questions.q: A quiz card reads: 'The Vedic janas were the Bharatas, Purus, Kurus, Yadus and Turvashas.' Give two reasons from the chapter why this card should not be read as the complete list.
questions.a: First, the Rig Veda alone lists over 30 janas, far more than five. Second, the chapter introduces the five with 'for instance' and ends with 'etc.', so they are only examples; and since it says 'the Rig Veda alone', other texts may add more.
s: The Rig Veda alone lists over 30 janas
The chapter gives the five only as examples ('for instance', 'etc.')

questions.q: A pupil reads the chapter's list of professions mentioned in the Vedic texts and writes four conclusions in her notebook. Which conclusion does the list actually support?
questions.a: The list runs from agriculturist to weaver, potter, builder, carpenter, healer, dancer, barber and priest, so it shows that many kinds of work were done. The list does not say how professions were shared out among janas, who chose them, or which was commonest.
o: People in Vedic times did many kinds of work besides farming
Every jana had at least one priest and one barber of its very own
The raja decided which profession each family would follow
Weaving was the commonest kind of work among the janas

questions.q:
On a heritage walk, a guide says five things about early Vedic society:
1. 'The Purus were one of the janas the Rig Veda lists.'
2. 'The people of a jana sometimes gathered together.'
3. 'Every jana had its own barber.'
4. 'The Yadus were linked to a region in the northwest of the Subcontinent.'
5. 'The samiti chose the raja by vote.'
Sort each remark as 'stated in the chapter', 'a fair inference from the chapter' or 'goes beyond the chapter', and give the reason for each.
questions.a: 1. Stated: the Purus are among the janas the Rig Veda lists. 2. Fair inference: the chapter says sabha and samiti refer to a collective gathering or assembly, so people did gather, though it does not describe how. 3. Goes beyond: the chapter says barbers are mentioned in the Vedic texts, not that every jana had one. 4. Stated: each clan was associated with a particular region of the northwest. 5. Goes beyond: the chapter gives samiti only as a clue-word and says not much is known of how the janas governed, so nothing about voting for the raja.
s: Remark 1: stated, the Purus are a listed jana
Remark 2: fair inference from sabha and samiti meaning a gathering
Remark 3: goes beyond, barbers are mentioned but not in every jana
Remark 4: stated, each clan linked to a northwest region
Remark 5: goes beyond, samiti is only a clue and governance is little known

questions.q: The chapter says ancient tribes were 'just different janas that lived in a specific environment'. It also gives the definition of a tribe that anthropologists use today. Compare the two: give one feature they share and two features that only the anthropologists' definition adds.
questions.a: Shared: both describe a group of people bound together as a clan or group of clans. Added by the anthropologists: a tradition of common descent, culture and language; living as a close-knit community under a chief; and holding no private property (any two). The ancient idea adds only that the jana lived in a specific environment, such as forests or mountains.
s: Shared feature: a clan or group of clans
First feature added by the anthropologists' definition
Second feature added by the anthropologists' definition

questions.q: In a Vedic-era hamlet, one person grows grain, one shapes clay pots, one cuts hair and one leads the offerings at a ritual. (a) Name each person's profession using the chapter's words. (b) The hamlet now wants to put up a new house with wooden doors. Using your answer to (a), which two professions from the chapter's list does it still need?
questions.a: (a) Agriculturist, potter, barber and priest. (b) None of those four builds; from the chapter's list the hamlet needs a builder for the house and a carpenter for the wooden doors.
s: Part (a): agriculturist, potter, barber, priest
Part (b): builder and carpenter, which are missing from the four

questions.q:
A school drama club is staging 'Shvetaketu and the seed of reality'. In their script, Shvetaketu leaves home for a gurukula at the age of 9 and stays as long as the chapter says. The prop box has only two items for the final scene: a banyan fruit cut open, and a small fire altar of the kind used for offerings to Agni.
(a) How old is Shvetaketu when he returns home? Show the working.
(b) What change in Shvetaketu does his father notice on his return, and on what topic does he question him?
(c) Which prop should the club use in the final scene? Justify the choice from Uddalaka's teaching.
questions.a: (a) He stays 12 years: 9 + 12 = 21 years old. (b) Uddalaka sees that he has become very proud of his learning and questions him on the nature of brahman, which Shvetaketu cannot answer. (c) The banyan fruit. Uddalaka explains that brahman, though invisible, is everywhere, just as the seed of a banyan fruit seems empty but already contains the future tree. The fire altar belongs to Vedic rituals to Agni, not to this teaching.
s: Part (a): 12 years, so 21 years old
Part (b): he had become proud; questioned on the nature of brahman
Part (c): the banyan fruit, because the seed that looks empty but holds the tree shows invisible brahman everywhere

questions.q: (a) What do the words 'rebirth' and 'karma' mean in the chapter? (b) Which group of texts introduced these ideas, and how were those texts related to the older Vedas?
questions.a: (a) Rebirth is taking birth again and again; karma is our actions or their results. (b) The Upanishads, which built upon Vedic concepts and introduced new ones.
s: Part (a): rebirth and karma correctly explained
Part (b): the Upanishads, which built on Vedic ideas

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Vedic schools of thought.
1. The Upanishads introduced the ideas of rebirth and karma.
2. According to the Upanishads, the atman in every being is ultimately one with brahman.
3. Yoga developed methods meant to achieve the realisation of brahman in one's consciousness.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three are what the chapter says.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: A pupil translates 'aham brahmasmi' as 'I am the god Brahma' and 'tat tvam asi' as 'You are that god Brahma'. What single error runs through both of her translations?
questions.a: The chapter says brahman, also called tat ('that'), is the one divine essence that everything is, and warns that it is not to be confused with the god Brahma. Both translations make exactly that confusion. 'Aham' rightly gives 'I' ('I am brahman'), 'tat' rightly gives 'that', and nothing in her translations calls the mantras Buddhist.
o: Reading brahman, the one divine essence, as the god Brahma
Reading 'aham' as 'I' when the mantra means 'you'
Treating two Vedantic mantras as Buddhist sayings
Taking 'tat' to mean 'that' when in the mantra it really means 'this'

questions.q: True or False? 'Yama was so pleased with Nachiketa's question about death that he answered it as soon as the boy asked.' Give the verdict and the corrected account from the Katha Upanishad story.
questions.a: False. Nachiketa met Yama only after a long wait, and Yama at first tried to avoid answering what happens after the death of the body. It was because the boy persisted that Yama was pleased, and only then did he explain that the atman is neither born nor dies.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Yama first avoided the question; pleased by the boy's persistence, he explained the atman

questions.q: A science teacher splits open a tiny banyan seed and says, 'It looks empty, yet a whole tree is already inside it.' A Sanskrit teacher says this is just how one Upanishadic teacher explained a big idea. Which idea?
questions.a: In the Chhandogya Upanishad, Uddalaka uses the banyan seed to show that brahman, though invisible, is everywhere. Karma and rebirth are other Upanishadic ideas, and the atman being neither born nor dying is Yama's teaching to Nachiketa.
o: Brahman is invisible but present everywhere
Our actions bring results, which is karma
A being is born again and again
The atman is neither born nor does it die

questions.q: (a) State what the Upanishads taught about the atman. (b) Explain why the chapter says it 'follows' from this that everything is connected, and name the prayer this explains.
questions.a: (a) The atman, or Self, is the divine essence that resides in every being and is ultimately one with brahman. (b) If the same divine essence is in every being, then all beings are connected and interdependent; this explains the prayer 'sarve bhavantu sukhinah', 'May all creatures be happy', free from disease and sorrow.
s: Part (a): atman is the divine Self in every being, one with brahman
Part (b): the same essence in all makes all connected, explaining 'May all creatures be happy'

questions.q: Dev says: 'The Upanishads rejected the Vedas, just as Buddhism did.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the Upanishads built upon Vedic concepts and introduced new ones, such as rebirth and karma, so they continued the Vedas rather than rejecting them. Vedanta and Yoga grew out of the Vedas and became foundations of what is now called Hinduism. It is Buddhism that did not accept the authority of the Vedas and developed its own system.
s: Verdict: disagree
The Upanishads built on Vedic concepts and added new ones
Buddhism, unlike them, did not accept the authority of the Vedas

questions.q: A pupil writes: 'aham brahmasmi means "I am brahman", and tat tvam asi means "I am That".' To match the chapter, the word 'I' in her second translation should be ___.
questions.a: You

questions.q: Kunal says, 'In Vedanta, brahman is present in people, but not in rivers, trees or stars.' Which statement from the chapter shows his mistake?
questions.a: Vedanta teaches that everything, human life, nature and the universe, is one divine essence called brahman, so rivers, trees and stars are included. The other options are not what Vedanta teaches in the chapter.
o: Everything, human life, nature and the universe, is brahman
Brahman is found only in those who perform the daily rituals
Brahman lives in nature, while people only have an atman
Brahman is present only in the seers who composed the hymns

questions.q:
Match each text or school in Column A with what the chapter connects it to in Column B.
Column A: 1. Chhandogya Upanishad  2. Katha Upanishad  3. Brihadaranyaka Upanishad  4. Yoga
Column B: a. methods to realise brahman in one's consciousness  b. a rishika questions a renowned rishi about brahman at a king's court  c. a son learns about brahman from a banyan seed and clay pots  d. a boy questions the god of death about the atman
questions.a: 1-c (Shvetaketu and Uddalaka), 2-d (Nachiketa and Yama), 3-b (Gargi and Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court), 4-a (Yoga's methods).

questions.q: Compare the stories of Shvetaketu and Nachiketa, and analyse what they share. Cover: how each one came to be taught, who taught him, what he learnt, and what the two stories have in common.
questions.a: Shvetaketu returned from 12 years at a gurukula proud of his learning; his father Uddalaka tested him on brahman and he could not answer. Uddalaka taught him that brahman, though invisible, is everywhere, like the banyan seed that holds the future tree or the many pots made of one clay: 'You are That, Shvetaketu.' Nachiketa angered his father with questions and was 'given' to Yama, the god of death; he waited, asked what happens after death and persisted until Yama explained that the atman, hidden in all creatures, is neither born nor dies. Both learn about the divine essence within everything, and both stories show the importance of asking questions: one is questioned, the other keeps questioning.
s: How Shvetaketu came to be taught, by Uddalaka
What Shvetaketu learnt: invisible brahman everywhere, 'You are That'
How Nachiketa came to be taught, by Yama
What Nachiketa learnt: the atman is neither born nor dies
What they share: the divine essence, and the importance of questions

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The prayer that begins 'sarve bhavantu sukhinah' wishes happiness for all creatures.
Reason (R): The Upanishads taught that each being has its own separate Self, unconnected to any other.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: the prayer means 'May all creatures be happy' and wishes them free from disease and sorrow. R is false: the Upanishads taught that the atman in every being is ultimately one with brahman, so everything is connected and interdependent.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Uddalaka used a banyan seed and pots made from one clay to teach that everything emerges from the same essence. Make up a new everyday example (not a seed and not clay) that could teach the same idea, and explain which part of your example stands for brahman and which parts stand for the many things of the world.
questions.a: Any fitting example, for instance: many ornaments (a ring, a bangle, a chain) are all made of the same gold; the gold stands for brahman, the one essence, and the different ornaments stand for the many different things that emerge from it. The answer should say that the many look different but share one essence.
s: A new example in which many things come from one material or source
Identifies what stands for brahman
Explains that the many things share that one essence

questions.q: A village holds a yajna so that everyone in it may be well, while one family nearby makes its own small daily offering at home. A pupil watching both is asked which pair of features matches the chapter's account of Vedic rituals.
questions.a: The chapter says rituals were directed towards deities for individual or collective benefit and wellbeing, and that the daily ones, generally offerings to Agni, became more and more complex in the course of time. Each wrong pair gets one half wrong: only one kind of benefit, Indra instead of Agni, or no growth in complexity.
o: Done for individual or collective benefit; grew more complex over time
Done only for collective benefit; grew simpler over time
Daily offerings made mostly to the deity Indra; grew more complex over time
Done only for individual benefit; stayed the same over time

questions.q: A student says, 'Yoga is only a set of body exercises.' (a) According to the chapter, what did Yoga develop methods for? (b) Using your answer to (a), explain why 'only body exercises' misses Yoga's aim, and say what brahman is according to the school of thought the chapter describes it under.
questions.a: (a) Methods intended to achieve the realisation of brahman in one's consciousness. (b) The aim is a change in awareness (consciousness), not only in the body. Brahman, in the school called Vedanta, is the one divine essence that everything, human life, nature and the universe, is.
s: Part (a): methods to realise brahman in one's consciousness
Part (b): the aim is in consciousness; brahman is Vedanta's one divine essence of everything

questions.q: Sana says: 'In the debate at King Janaka's court, Yajnavalkya refused to answer Gargi's question about brahman.' Is she right? Test her claim against the story.
questions.a: Partly right. At first, after Gargi's series of questions on the nature of the world and finally on brahman, Yajnavalkya did ask her to stop asking further questions. But the story goes on: later Gargi resumed her questions and Yajnavalkya explained how brahman makes the world, the seasons, the rivers and everything else possible. So he did answer in the end.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: he asked her to stop at first
Wrong part: she resumed and he explained brahman

questions.q: A pupil says, 'In the Upanishadic stories, only grown men ask the big questions.' Using the stories in the chapter, show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: The chapter introduces the stories by saying they show the importance of asking questions, whether they come from men, women or children. Gargi, a rishika (a woman), asked Yajnavalkya a series of questions on the world and on brahman, and resumed them even after he asked her to stop. Nachiketa, a boy, kept asking his father and then persisted with Yama until Yama explained the atman. So questions come from a woman and a child as well as from men.
s: Gargi, a rishika, questioned Yajnavalkya on brahman
Nachiketa, a boy, persisted with his questions to Yama
Conclusion, with the chapter's 'men, women or children'

questions.q: A pupil explains the Upanishadic ideas of brahman and atman by comparing them to the ocean and a single wave. (a) Which of the two ideas does the ocean stand for, and which does the wave stand for? (b) Using your answer to (a), explain one way the comparison fits what the Upanishads say about the atman.
questions.a: (a) The ocean stands for brahman, the one divine essence of everything; the wave stands for the atman, the Self in one being. (b) A wave is a separate shape but is made of the same water as the ocean, just as the atman resides in each being but is ultimately one with brahman.
s: Part (a): ocean is brahman, wave is atman
Part (b): the wave is the same water, as the atman is ultimately one with brahman

questions.q:
A pupil's flow chart 'From Vedic rituals to schools of thought' has five boxes:
Box 1: Daily rituals, mostly offerings to Indra, stay simple over time.
Box 2: The Upanishads build on Vedic concepts and add rebirth and karma.
Box 3: Vedanta: everything is brahman, which is another name for the god Brahma.
Box 4: Yoga develops methods to realise brahman in one's consciousness.
Box 5: Buddhism grows out of these schools and becomes a foundation of Hinduism.
Check each box against the chapter: write 'correct' with a reason, or rewrite the box as the chapter has it.
questions.a: Box 1 is wrong: daily rituals were generally offerings to Agni, and they became more and more complex over time. Box 2 is correct: the Upanishads built upon Vedic concepts and introduced rebirth and karma. Box 3 is wrong: Vedanta says everything is one divine essence, brahman, which is not to be confused with the god Brahma. Box 4 is correct: Yoga developed methods to realise brahman in one's consciousness. Box 5 is wrong: Buddhism did not accept the authority of the Vedas; it was Vedanta, Yoga and the other schools that grew out of the Vedas that became foundations for what we call Hinduism.
s: Box 1 rewritten: offerings to Agni, growing more complex
Box 2 judged correct, with reason
Box 3 rewritten: brahman is not the god Brahma
Box 4 judged correct, with reason
Box 5 rewritten: Buddhism rejected Vedic authority; the Vedic schools founded Hinduism

questions.q:
For a library poster on Vedanta, three pupils drafted captions for the mantra 'tat tvam asi':
Card P: '"You are That": Uddalaka's closing words to Shvetaketu; it means the boy is the god Brahma.'
Card Q: '"You are That": Yama's words to Nachiketa; it means the Self in you is one with the divine essence of everything.'
Card R: '"You are That": Uddalaka's closing words to Shvetaketu, who had come home from the gurukula humble and eager to learn; everything consists of one subtle essence.'
The librarian's rule: a wrong meaning is the worst error, a wrong speaker is the next worst, and a wrong background detail is the least serious.
(a) Find the error in Card P.
(b) Find the error in Card Q.
(c) Find the error in Card R.
(d) Using the librarian's rule, which card should be corrected and printed? Justify by ranking all three.
questions.a: (a) The meaning: 'That' (tat) is brahman, the divine essence, which the chapter says is not to be confused with the god Brahma. (b) The speaker: 'You are That' is Uddalaka's conclusion to Shvetaketu; Yama taught Nachiketa that the atman is neither born nor dies. (c) The background detail: Shvetaketu came home after 12 years very proud of his learning, not humble. (d) Card R. Its speaker and meaning are right and its error is only a background detail, the least serious; Card Q's meaning is right but its speaker is wrong; Card P's meaning is wrong, the worst error. Ranking: R, then Q, then P.
s: Part (a): P's meaning wrong, tat is brahman not the god Brahma
Part (b): Q's speaker wrong, the words are Uddalaka's to Shvetaketu
Part (c): R's detail wrong, Shvetaketu returned proud
Part (d): Card R, ranked R, Q, P under the rule

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Siddhartha Gautama decided to give up his palace life.
Reason (R): Siddhartha Gautama was born a prince, in Lumbini.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. But being born a prince is not why he left: the chapter says he decided to give up palace life following the chariot ride at 29, when he saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a peaceful ascetic. So R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Five cards from a pupil's storyboard on the Buddha are jumbled:
P: He meditates for many days under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya.
Q: On a chariot ride he sees an old man, a sick man, a dead body and an ascetic.
R: He founds the Sangha.
S: He travels on foot, meeting other ascetics and scholars.
T: He grows up living a protected life in the palace.
Put the cards in the chapter's order. Then, for each of the four links between neighbouring cards, explain what in the earlier card led to the later one.
questions.a: Order: T, Q, S, P, R. T to Q: because his palace life was protected, the ride at 29 was the first time in his life he met old age, sickness and death. Q to S: having seen suffering, and an ascetic who seemed happy and at peace, he gave up palace life and became a wandering ascetic searching for the root cause of suffering. S to P: the search led to many days of meditation, after which he attained enlightenment, realising that ignorance and attachment are the source of suffering, and became the Buddha. P to R: having realised this, he started teaching, and founded the Sangha of monks (later nuns) to practise and spread his teachings.
s: Correct order T, Q, S, P, R
Link T to Q: a protected life, so the sights were new to him
Link Q to S: suffering and a peaceful ascetic led him to leave and search
Link S to P: the search ended in enlightenment about ignorance and attachment
Link P to R: he began teaching and founded the Sangha to spread it

questions.q: A travel blogger's itinerary 'In the footsteps of the Buddha' has three stops: Lumbini (Nepal), Bodh Gaya (Bihar) and Vaishali (Bihar). Which change makes the itinerary fit the chapter?
questions.a: Siddhartha was born in Lumbini (today in Nepal) and attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya (today in Bihar). Vaishali is where the chapter places the birth of Prince Vardhamana, Mahavira, so it does not belong on this route.
o: Drop Vaishali: the chapter links it to Vardhamana's birth
Drop Bodh Gaya: the chapter puts his enlightenment at Lumbini
Drop Lumbini: the chapter says he was born near Vaishali
Keep all three, but say that Bodh Gaya is in Nepal

questions.q: True or False? 'Siddhartha attained enlightenment soon after he left the palace.' Give the verdict and the corrected account.
questions.a: False. After leaving, he travelled on foot as an ascetic, meeting other ascetics and scholars and searching for the root cause of suffering; only after meditating for many days under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya did he attain enlightenment.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a long search as an ascetic, then many days of meditation at Bodh Gaya

questions.q: A pupil draws a tree of schools of thought and puts Buddhism on a branch growing out of the Vedas, next to Yoga. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says Yoga and several other schools grew out of the Vedas, but Buddhism was one of the schools that did not accept the authority of the Vedas and developed its own system. It does not say Buddhism came from Jainism or Vedanta, and the Vedas are the oldest texts of India.
o: Buddhism did not accept the Vedas' authority and built its own system
Buddhism grew out of Jainism, so it belongs on the Jain branch
Buddhism is older than the Vedas, so it is the tree's trunk
Buddhism was a part of Vedanta, so it belongs on the same branch as Vedanta

questions.q: (a) What does the name 'Buddha' mean? (b) What does this name tell us about what happened to Siddhartha under the pipal tree at Bodh Gaya?
questions.a: (a) The 'enlightened' or 'awakened' one. (b) That he attained enlightenment there: he realised that ignorance (avidya) and attachment are the source of human suffering and conceived a method to remove them, and so came to be called the Buddha.
s: Part (a): the enlightened or awakened one
Part (b): he attained enlightenment there, realising the causes of suffering

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Buddha.
1. Siddhartha first saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body and an ascetic at the age of 30.
2. 'Buddha' means the enlightened or awakened one.
3. Siddhartha meditated for many days under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya, today in Bihar.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false: the chapter says he was 29 when he took the chariot ride and saw these four sights; 30 is the age at which Vardhamana left home.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A film script shows young Siddhartha visiting sick villagers outside the palace many times before he was 29. Which point in the chapter does this scene contradict?
questions.a: The chapter says he grew up living a protected life in the palace, and that on the chariot ride at 29 he came across an old man, a sick man and a dead body for the first time in his life. Earlier visits to the sick would contradict that. The other points are in the chapter but say nothing about what he saw before 29.
o: At 29 he met a sick man for the first time in his life
He was born a prince in Lumbini, today in Nepal
He left behind his wife and son when he left the palace
He meditated for many days under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya

questions.q: Interpret the Buddha's saying: 'Conquering oneself is greater than conquering a thousand men on the battlefield a thousand times.' (a) What does 'conquering oneself' mean here? (b) Which emphasis in the Buddha's teaching does the saying express?
questions.a: (a) Mastering one's own mind, desires and habits, rather than defeating others. (b) His insistence on a sincere inner discipline: the chapter says this saying expresses that emphasis simply.
s: Part (a): mastering oneself rather than others
Part (b): the emphasis on sincere inner discipline

questions.q: A boy cannot sleep because he fears losing his new cricket bat. Of the two causes of suffering Siddhartha realised at Bodh Gaya, the one troubling the boy is ___.
questions.a: attachment

questions.q: Aditi claims: 'For the Buddha, purity was about what is inside a person, not about outward acts such as bathing in a sacred river.' Is her claim supported by the chapter? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The Buddha said, 'Not by water is one made pure, though many people may bathe here. But one is pure in whom truth and dharma reside', so purity depends on truth and dharma within a person. This fits his insistence on a sincere inner discipline, and his saying that conquering oneself is greater than conquering a thousand men a thousand times.
s: Verdict: supported
Uses the saying that water does not make one pure; truth and dharma do
Links it to his emphasis on inner discipline

questions.q: A writer says, 'People suffer only because they are born poor.' Which idea from the Buddha's enlightenment challenges this?
questions.a: At Bodh Gaya Siddhartha realised that avidya (ignorance) and attachment are the source of human suffering. The other options are not what the chapter says the Buddha realised; the last one is closer to the Charvaka school's view of the world.
o: Ignorance and attachment are the source of suffering
The anger of the deities is the source of suffering
Skipping the daily rituals is the source of suffering
This material world, the only thing that exists, causes it

questions.q: (a) Siddhartha, travelling on foot after leaving the palace, and a bhikshu of the Sangha: which of the chapter's words, 'ascetic' or 'monk', does the chapter use for each? (b) Using your answer to (a), what does the chapter's meaning of 'monk' add that its meaning of 'ascetic' does not?
questions.a: (a) Siddhartha travelled as an ascetic, someone who engages in a rigorous discipline to attain a higher consciousness; a bhikshu is a monk. (b) A monk gives up the usual life in the world and usually takes vows, committing himself to follow strict rules for a disciplined life; the meaning of ascetic speaks only of rigorous discipline.
s: Part (a): Siddhartha an ascetic; a bhikshu a monk
Part (b): a monk gives up worldly life and usually takes vows to follow strict rules

questions.q: A student writes: 'The Sangha was the Buddha's royal army.' (a) Correct the statement. (b) Explain why an army would go against two of the Buddha's teachings given in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Sangha was a community of bhikshus (monks) and, later, bhikshunis (nuns) who dedicated themselves to practising and spreading the Buddha's teachings. (b) An army hurts and injures, which goes against ahimsa, non-hurting; and the Buddha taught that conquering oneself is greater than conquering a thousand men on the battlefield a thousand times, so outer conquest was not his aim.
s: Part (a): a community of monks and later nuns spreading his teachings
Part (b): an army breaks ahimsa and puts outer conquest above conquering oneself

questions.q: Pooja never hits anyone, but she often wishes that bad things would happen to a classmate she dislikes. Would the chapter say she fully follows ahimsa as Buddhism understands it? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. Ahimsa originally means non-hurting or non-injuring, not just avoiding physical violence. The chapter adds that in Buddhism (and Jainism) it means much more than refraining from physical violence: it also means refraining from violence in thought, such as ill feelings towards anyone. By noticing such thoughts she could learn to turn them into positive ones.
s: Verdict: no, she does not fully follow it
Ahimsa means non-hurting, more than avoiding physical violence
It includes refraining from violence in thought, such as ill feelings

questions.q: On his chariot ride at 29, Siddhartha saw four sights. (a) How was the ascetic different from the other three? (b) How does this difference show up in what Siddhartha did next?
questions.a: (a) The old man, the sick man and the dead body showed suffering, while the ascetic appeared happy and at peace. (b) Siddhartha gave up his palace life and himself travelled on foot as an ascetic, searching for the root cause of suffering.
s: Part (a): the ascetic seemed happy and at peace, the other three showed suffering
Part (b): he became a wandering ascetic searching for the cause of suffering

questions.q: A school play shows the Sangha in two scenes: one in its first years and one some years later. Which description of its members across the two scenes fits the chapter?
questions.a: The Sangha was a community of bhikshus, or monks, and later of bhikshunis, or nuns, who dedicated themselves to practising and spreading the Buddha's teachings. Yajnas were Vedic rituals, and the chapter gives no order of nuns before monks and no role guarding a king.
o: Monks first, nuns later; both devoted to practising and spreading the teachings
Monks and nuns together from the very start; all devoted to performing yajnas
Nuns first, monks later; both devoted to spreading the teachings
Monks only, never nuns; all devoted to guarding the king

questions.q: A pupil argues: 'When Siddhartha left behind his wife and son, he had already overcome attachment, long before Bodh Gaya.' Test this claim against the order of events in the chapter.
questions.a: Not supported. The chapter says that after the four sights he decided to give up palace life and then travelled as an ascetic searching for the root cause of suffering. It was only after meditating for many days under the pipal tree at Bodh Gaya that he realised ignorance and attachment are the source of suffering. The claim reads that later realisation back into an earlier step; the chapter says only that he left.
s: Verdict: not supported
He left to search for the cause of suffering, not yet knowing it
Attachment was named as a cause only at enlightenment at Bodh Gaya

questions.q: Compare the Buddha's teaching with the Vedic schools of thought described in the chapter, and analyse what they share and where they part. Use five points.
questions.a: 1. Buddhism was one of the schools that did not accept the authority of the Vedas and developed its own system, while Vedanta and Yoga grew out of the Vedas. 2. The Buddha located the cause of suffering in avidya (ignorance) and attachment and conceived a method to remove them. 3. He stressed ahimsa, non-hurting, and a sincere inner discipline rather than outward acts such as bathing in sacred rivers. 4. Yet the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools shared concepts such as dharma, karma, rebirth and the search for an end to suffering and ignorance. 5. Ahimsa is shared to a large extent with the Vedantic school, so the schools differ on the authority of the Vedas but share a common trunk of values.
s: Buddhism rejected the Vedas' authority; Vedanta and Yoga grew out of them
The Buddha's cause of suffering: ignorance and attachment
Ahimsa and inner discipline over outward acts
Shared concepts: dharma, karma, rebirth, ending suffering
Conclusion: they differ on authority but share values

questions.q:
A school heritage club in 2026 owns four objects about the Buddha: (1) a stone panel, about 1,800 years old, showing the Buddha teaching; (2) a copy of a painting from the Ajanta caves showing the Buddha teaching; (3) a model of a rock-cut cave with stone beds, labelled 'home of monks who travelled from afar to spread the teaching'; (4) a statue of the Buddha from Bhutan.
(a) In about which century CE was object (1) made? Show the working.
(b) What does object (3) tell visitors about how some Buddhist monks lived and worked?
(c) Only two objects can go to a small travelling show titled 'The Buddha's teaching travelled far'. Which two should go? Justify the choice.
questions.a: (a) 2026 - 1,800 = about 226 CE, so about the 3rd century CE. (b) Monks travelled across the land to spread the teachings; some led ascetic lives in caves cut in the rock and slept on stone beds, and archaeologists have even found the names of monks who lived in such caves. (c) Objects (3) and (4). The cave model shows monks travelling and settling in faraway places to spread the teachings, and the statue from Bhutan shows the teaching present outside India, in Asia. Objects (1) and (2) show the Buddha teaching but not how far the teaching travelled.
s: Part (a): about 226 CE, the 3rd century CE
Part (b): travelling monks living ascetic lives in rock-cut caves
Part (c): objects (3) and (4), because they show travel and spread beyond India

questions.q:
A teacher is telling Class 6 a Jataka tale. She stops at this point: 'A king's soldiers found the huge tree whose fruit had floated down the stream, and attacked the troop of monkeys living there. The monkeys could not cross the stream on their own ...'
(a) The monkey-king had ordered that no fruit should escape. Explain how the one fruit that escaped led to the attack.
(b) Why could the monkey-king, and not one of the others, save the troop, and what did it cost him?
(c) The tale ends with the watching king thinking. What did he think about, and why does a tale of the Buddha's former birth fit such an ending?
(d) Two morals are proposed: 'A leader should put the safety of those in his care above his own' and 'One careless mistake can bring danger to the whole group'. Both fit parts of the story. Which fits the way the tale ends better? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The fruit fell into the stream, was carried by the current, caught in a net and taken to the palace; the king loved its taste and sent soldiers to find the tree, and they found and attacked the monkeys. (b) He was much larger than them, so he could hold a tree on the other bank and let them use his body as a bridge; he was severely bruised and eventually died. (c) He was moved by the selfless sacrifice and thought about the role of a king towards his subjects; Jataka tales tell of the Buddha's former births and express Buddhist values in simple terms. (d) The first moral. The second fits the start of the story, but the tale ends with a ruler reflecting on a ruler's duty after watching a leader give his life for his troop.
s: Part (a): the escaped fruit reached the palace and the king sent soldiers to find the tree
Part (b): his size let him be a bridge; bruised and died
Part (c): the king thought about his role towards subjects; Jatakas express Buddhist values
Part (d): the leadership moral, because the ending is the king reflecting on a ruler's duty

questions.q:
Read the statements about Jainism.
1. Vardhamana was born near the city of Vaishali, in modern-day Bihar.
2. Jainism holds that only humans and large animals depend on one another.
3. According to the chapter, Jainism began only when the Buddha started teaching.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 1 is correct. Statement 2 is false: Jainism insists on the interdependence of all creatures, from humans to invisible organisms. Statement 3 is false: Jainism became widespread at the same time as Buddhism, but its roots are said to be much more ancient.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Mahavira said: 'All breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away.' (a) Which Jain teaching does this saying illustrate? (b) Which other Jain idea about creatures gives a reason for treating all of them in this way? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Ahimsa, non-hurting. (b) The interconnectedness and interdependence of all creatures: from humans to invisible organisms, they support each other and cannot live without one another, so harming any of them harms the whole web of life.
s: Part (a): ahimsa
Part (b): all creatures are interconnected and interdependent, so none should be harmed

questions.q: A teacher draws a chart titled 'Ideas shared by the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools'. Which entry should NOT be on the chart?
questions.a: The chapter says the three schools shared dharma, karma, rebirth and the search for an end to suffering and ignorance. The view that there is no life after death belonged to the Charvaka school, so it does not belong on the chart.
o: No life after death
Karma, our actions or their results
Rebirth, taking birth again and again
The search for an end to suffering

questions.q:
The chapter says only that Prince Vardhamana was born in the early 6th century BCE. For a timeline poster, a class decides to suppose that he was born in 599 BCE. They then use the chapter's ages and time periods for the rest of his early life. One pupil writes the year he left home as 629 BCE.
(a) In which year BCE would he have left home? Show the working.
(b) In which year BCE would he have achieved supreme wisdom? Show the working.
(c) Explain the pupil's mistake with 629 BCE.
(d) Does 599 BCE fit the chapter's phrase 'early 6th century BCE'? Justify your judgement.
questions.a: (a) He left home at 30: 599 - 30 = 569 BCE. (b) After 12 years of ascetic discipline: 569 - 12 = 557 BCE. (c) BCE years count down towards 1 CE, so later events have smaller BCE numbers; the pupil added 30 instead of subtracting it. (d) Yes. The 6th century BCE runs from 600 to 501 BCE, and 599 BCE is right at its start, so it is 'early' in that century.
s: Part (c): BCE numbers fall as time passes, so 30 must be subtracted
Part (d): yes, 599 BCE is at the start of 600-501 BCE

questions.q: Three friends describe the same hill. Asha, who sees it from the forest side, calls it green; Ben, who sees the quarry side, calls it rocky; Chitra, who saw it in winter, calls it misty. Their teacher says each is partly right and no single description is complete. Which teaching from the chapter is the teacher using?
questions.a: Anekantavada, a Jain teaching: the truth has many aspects and cannot be fully described by any single statement. Aparigraha is non-possession, ahimsa is non-hurting, and aham brahmasmi is the Vedantic mantra "I am brahman".
o: Anekantavada
Aparigraha
Ahimsa
Aham brahmasmi

questions.q: Kiran says: 'Jainism and Buddhism did not accept the authority of the Vedas, so they shared nothing with the Vedic schools.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Rejecting the Vedas' authority did not mean sharing nothing. The chapter says the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools shared concepts such as dharma, karma, rebirth and the search for an end to suffering and ignorance. It also says the Jain teachings of ahimsa, anekantavada and aparigraha are shared to a large extent with Buddhism and the Vedantic school.
s: Verdict: disagree
Shared concepts: dharma, karma, rebirth, ending suffering and ignorance
Jain teachings shared to a large extent with Buddhism and Vedanta

questions.q: Counting from his birth, the chapter's figures for Prince Vardhamana put his achieving 'infinite knowledge' at about the age of ___.
A poster in a school corridor shows Mahavira with the caption 'The great conqueror'. A visitor asks which lands he conquered. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: 'Jain' comes from jina, conqueror, but the chapter says this refers to the conquest of ignorance and attachments to reach enlightenment, not of territory or enemies. Vardhamana was a prince, but the chapter does not say he conquered janas, ruled Vaishali or defeated the Buddha.
o: None; he conquered ignorance and attachments
The janas of the northwest, one after another
The city of Vaishali, which he then ruled
The Buddha's followers, in a great debate

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter calls Buddhism and Jainism 'religions' because that word describes them fully.
Reason (R): These schools of thought have philosophical, spiritual, religious, ethical and social aspects.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the chapter deliberately avoids the word 'religion', preferring 'schools of thought' and 'belief systems', because many scholars find 'religion' too limiting for the Indian civilisation. R is true: it is the chapter's reason for avoiding the word.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Before moving to a hostel, four students pack in different ways. Whose choice goes AGAINST aparigraha?
questions.a: Aparigraha means non-possession: detachment from material possessions, limiting oneself to what is truly necessary. Buying extra gadgets that are not needed goes against it; giving away, keeping only what is needed and sharing all fit it.
o: Lata buys three new gadgets she does not need
Arif gives away clothes he has outgrown
Sunita keeps only the books she needs this year
Dev shares one bicycle with his neighbour

questions.q: True or False? 'The rock-cut caves at Ellora are where the travelling Jain and Buddhist monks of Mahavira's own time, the 6th century BCE, lived.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the caves at Ellora (Maharashtra) were cut between the 6th and the 10th centuries CE, more than a thousand years after Mahavira, who was born in the early 6th century BCE; some of them are Hindu, others Buddhist and Jain.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Ellora was cut in the 6th to 10th centuries CE, not BCE, with Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves

questions.q: At Bharhut in Madhya Pradesh, a guide points to a stone panel showing a large monkey stretched across a stream while smaller monkeys walk over his body. Which tradition's values is the panel's story meant to express, and how?
questions.a: The chapter says the Bharhut panel depicts the story of the monkey-king, a Jataka tale; Jataka tales tell stories of the Buddha's former births and express Buddhist values in simple terms. The story is not from Mahavira's life, a Vedic hymn, or the Buddha's own life at Bodh Gaya.
o: Buddhist values, through a tale of the Buddha's former birth
Jain values, through Mahavira's early life as a prince
Vedic values, through a hymn sung to the deity Agni
Buddhist values, through the story of the Buddha's own life at Bodh Gaya

questions.q: (a) Give one way in which the early lives of Vardhamana and Siddhartha Gautama were alike. (b) Give two differences between them, from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Both were born into royal families as princes, and both left home in search of spiritual knowledge. (b) Any two: Vardhamana was born near Vaishali (Bihar), Siddhartha in Lumbini (Nepal); Vardhamana achieved supreme wisdom after 12 years of ascetic discipline, Siddhartha attained enlightenment after meditating for many days under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya; Vardhamana became known as Mahavira, 'great hero', Siddhartha as the Buddha, 'the enlightened one'.
s: Part (a): both royal princes who left home
Part (b): two differences of birthplace, path to wisdom or title

questions.q: A travel blog says the rock-cut caves of Ellora belong to a single tradition. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the caves at Ellora (Maharashtra) were cut between the 6th and the 10th centuries CE, and some are Hindu, others Buddhist and Jain. The distractors keep only one tradition or move the date to the BCE period.
o: Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves, cut in the 6th-10th centuries CE
Only Buddhist caves, cut between the 6th and the 10th centuries CE
Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves, cut in the 6th century BCE
Only Jain caves, cut by Mahavira's first group of monks

questions.q: The Charvaka school 'does not seem to have gained much popularity and it disappeared with time'. (a) What did the Charvaka school believe? (b) Why, then, does the chapter bother to mention it?
questions.a: (a) That this material world is the only thing that exists, so there can be no life after death. (b) To show that there was a wide diversity of intellectual or spiritual belief systems, and that people were free to choose what suited them.
s: Part (a): only the material world exists, no life after death
Part (b): to show the wide diversity of belief systems and freedom to choose

questions.q: In which story from the chapter does the same piece of knowledge first help a man escape punishment and then lead him to give himself up?
questions.a: Rohineya, remembering a few sentences of Mahavira's sermon, saw through the minister's plan to make him confess; later, remorseful, he went to Mahavira, confessed and returned the stolen treasures. Nachiketa and Shvetaketu were not escaping punishment, and the monkey-king gave his life rather than escaping.
o: The Jain story of Rohineya
The story of Nachiketa and Yama
The story of Shvetaketu and the seed
The Jataka tale of the monkey-king

questions.q: (a) How did a few sentences of Mahavira's sermon help Rohineya after he was arrested? (b) What did Rohineya do afterwards that shows the 'right action and right thinking' the chapter says the story illustrates?
questions.a: (a) Remembering Mahavira's words, he was able to detect the minister's clever plan to make him confess and defeat it. (b) Feeling remorseful, he went to Mahavira, confessed his crimes, returned the stolen treasures, asked for forgiveness and became a monk focused on higher knowledge.
s: Part (a): the words helped him see through and defeat the minister's trap
Part (b): he confessed, returned the treasures, sought forgiveness and became a monk

questions.q: Interpret why the chapter prefers the terms 'schools of thought' and 'belief systems' to the word 'religion'. Give three points.
questions.a: 1. A school of thought, as the chapter defines it, is a group of thinkers or spiritual seekers who share similar ideas about human life and the world, which is wider than worship alone. 2. These schools have many aspects: philosophical, spiritual, religious, ethical and social. 3. Many scholars agree that the word 'religion' is too limiting in the context of the Indian civilisation, so a wider term is used.
s: Meaning of a school of thought: thinkers sharing ideas about life and the world
The schools have philosophical, spiritual, religious, ethical and social aspects
Scholars find 'religion' too limiting for the Indian civilisation

questions.q: The word 'Jain' comes from jina, 'conqueror', and the Buddha said, 'Conquering oneself is greater than conquering a thousand men on the battlefield a thousand times.' Compare the two ideas of conquest: say what is conquered in each, and what the two share.
questions.a: Jina refers not to conquering territory or enemies but to conquering ignorance and attachments, so as to reach enlightenment. The Buddha's saying places conquering oneself above any victory over others, expressing his insistence on inner discipline. Both turn conquest inward; and the Buddha himself found ignorance and attachment to be the source of suffering, the very things the jina conquers.
s: Jina: conquest of ignorance and attachments, not territory
Buddha: conquering oneself, inner discipline, above battlefield victory
Shared: inward conquest of ignorance and attachment

questions.q: The school magazine asks you for a short piece titled 'Three Jain ideas for today'. Write its key points: explain ahimsa, anekantavada and aparigraha as the chapter does, give one present-day example of each that shows the idea being applied, and end with one connection you see between the three ideas, argued in a sentence.
questions.a: Ahimsa: non-hurting, which in Jainism extends to all creatures and even to violent thoughts; example: not mistreating stray animals. Anekantavada: truth has many aspects and no single statement says it all; example: listening to both sides in a class quarrel. Aparigraha: non-possession, limiting oneself to what is truly necessary; example: not buying things one does not need. Connection: any reasonable link argued from the ideas, for example that all three ask a person to hold back (from harm, from insisting on one view, from owning more), or that the chapter says all three are shared to a large extent with Buddhism and Vedanta.
s: Ahimsa explained as the chapter does, with an applied example
Anekantavada explained as the chapter does, with an applied example
Aparigraha explained as the chapter does, with an applied example
Each example applies the idea to a present-day situation rather than restating it
A connection between the three, argued in a sentence

questions.q:
Copy and complete this table for three schools of thought named in the chapter, then answer the two questions below it.
Rows: Vedanta | Jainism | Charvaka
Column 1: What it held about life after death or rebirth
Column 2: One idea or teaching of its own
(i) Fill in each row (one mark per row).
(ii) Which school stands apart from the other two in Column 1?
