(iii) What does the chapter say the existence of such different schools shows about people at the time?
questions.a: Vedanta: the Upanishads introduced rebirth, and the atman is neither born nor dies; its own idea: everything is one divine essence, brahman. Jainism: rebirth is one of the concepts the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools shared; its own teachings: ahimsa, anekantavada or aparigraha. Charvaka (Lokayata): this material world is the only thing that exists, so there can be no life after death; that is also its own idea. (ii) Charvaka, which denies any life after death while the other two accept rebirth. (iii) There was a wide diversity of intellectual or spiritual belief systems, and people were free to choose what suited them.
s: Vedanta row: rebirth or the undying atman; brahman
Jainism row: shared rebirth; ahimsa, anekantavada or aparigraha
Charvaka row: only the material world, no life after death
Charvaka stands apart in Column 1
Wide diversity, and freedom to choose what suited them

questions.q:
A school garden club sprayed a strong insecticide on its vegetable beds. The club's records: bee visits counted in one morning fell from 120 before spraying to 15 after; the season's vegetable harvest fell from 40 kg the year before to 25 kg. For next season it must choose. Plan A: spray again, 4 sprays at Rs 450 each, about 2 hours of work per spray, and leaves free of insects. Plan B: pick pests off by hand, no cost in money, but 4 volunteers working 1.5 hours each, twice a week, for 16 weeks, and last year's hand-picked trial bed still lost about one leaf in five to pests.
(a) By how many kilograms did the harvest fall, and what fraction of the earlier harvest is this?
(b) How many volunteer-hours does Plan B need, and how many more hours is that than Plan A?
(c) Which Jain idea about creatures do the bee and harvest records illustrate? Explain using the chapter.
(d) Plan A is cheaper in time and keeps the leaves cleaner. Which plan fits Jain teaching, and what cost must the club accept to follow it? Justify using ahimsa and your answer to (c).
questions.a: (a) 40 - 25 = 15 kg, which is 15/40 = 3/8 of the earlier harvest. (b) 4 x 1.5 x 2 x 16 = 192 volunteer-hours; Plan A needs 4 x 2 = 8 hours, so Plan B needs 184 more hours. (c) The interconnectedness and interdependence of all creatures: from humans to invisible organisms, creatures support each other and cannot live without one another, which the chapter says scientists have confirmed; harming insects also hurt the bees and, through them, the harvest. (d) Plan B. Ahimsa asks that living creatures not be slain or harmed, and (c) shows that harming small creatures harms the whole garden. The club must accept 184 extra hours of work and some leaves lost to pests.
s: Part (a): 15 kg, 3/8 of the earlier harvest
Part (b): 192 volunteer-hours, 184 more than Plan A's 8
Part (c): interdependence of all creatures, confirmed by scientists
Part (d): Plan B, by ahimsa and interdependence, accepting the extra hours and some leaf loss

questions.q: True or False? 'Folk and tribal traditions count among India's cultural roots because they were later written down in texts, like the other schools of thought.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Folk and tribal traditions are oral traditions, passed on through everyday practice without written texts. They count among India's cultural roots because of their long, two-way interaction with the leading schools of thought, which the chapter calls mutual enrichment.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: they are oral, passed on through practice, and count as roots because of mutual enrichment

questions.q: A guide at Puri tells visitors: 'Historians have proved from written records that Jagannath began as a tribal deity.' Which correction matches the chapter's own wording?
questions.a: The chapter says that, according to tradition, Jagannath, worshipped at Puri (Odisha), was originally a tribal deity, as were various forms of the mother-goddess. It cites tradition, not written proof, and it does not link Jagannath to the Vedic hymns or the Todas.
o: The chapter says this is so 'according to tradition', not proven by records
The chapter says Jagannath began as a deity praised in the Vedic hymns
The chapter says Jagannath was first worshipped by the Todas of the Nilgiris
The chapter says only the mother-goddess forms, not Jagannath, were tribal

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Deities, legends and rituals have passed freely, for a very long time, between tribal traditions and the leading schools of thought.
Reason (R): Folk, tribal and Hindu belief systems share many concepts, such as regarding mountains, rivers, trees and animals as sacred.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and the chapter asks how such interactions took place for so long and so naturally and answers that it is because these belief systems have many similar concepts. So R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What terms does the Constitution of India use for tribes, in English and in Hindi? (b) Why could the Constitution not simply borrow an ancient Indian word for 'tribe'?
questions.a: (a) 'Tribes' and 'tribal communities' in English, and janjati in Hindi. (b) Ancient India did not have a word for 'tribe': tribes were just different janas that lived in a specific environment, such as forests or mountains.
s: Part (a): tribes and tribal communities; janjati
Part (b): ancient India had no word for tribe, only janas in a specific environment

questions.q: On a trek in the Nilgiris, Aman points his finger at a mountain peak to show it to his friend. A Toda elder walking with them looks upset. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: For the Toda tribals of the Nilgiris, over thirty peaks are residences of a god or a goddess, and they are so sacred that the Todas avoid pointing to them with a finger. The other options misuse ideas from the chapter: a tribe holds no private property, and Singbonga belongs to eastern India.
o: The peak is a deity's home, too sacred to point at
The peak is the chief's private property
Pointing is how a Toda challenges a raja
The peak is where Singbonga made the world

questions.q:
Read the statements about tribes in India.
1. In Hindi, the Constitution of India uses the word janjati for tribes.
2. According to official figures, India had 705 tribes in 2011.
3. Ancient India had its own distinct word for 'tribe', separate from jana.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: ancient India did not have a word for 'tribe'; tribes were just different janas living in a specific environment.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A grandmother in a Bihar village teaches her granddaughter a harvest song she learnt by ear; a Toda elder teaches a child which Nilgiri peaks must never be pointed at. (a) Classify each as a folk or a tribal tradition, giving the chapter's basis. (b) Using your answer to (a), name the larger group of traditions both belong to, and the ancient texts the chapter says were passed on in the same way.
questions.a: (a) The song is a folk tradition, transmitted by common people; the Toda teaching is a tribal tradition, transmitted by a tribe. (b) Both are oral traditions, teachings or practices passed on through everyday practice without written texts; the chapter says this is also the case of the Vedas.
s: Part (a): song folk (common people), Toda teaching tribal (a tribe)
Part (b): both oral traditions without written texts, like the Vedas

questions.q: A modern writer argues that because tribes hold no private property and pass on their traditions orally, the 19th-century label 'primitive' still fits them. Which point from the chapter best answers her?
questions.a: The chapter says 19th-century anthropologists often called tribes 'primitive' or 'inferior', but with deeper studies of their rich and complex cultures such biased judgments have been mostly abandoned. Holding no private property is part of today's definition of a tribe, and the chapter says nothing about the Constitution banning the word or about small tribes.
o: Deeper studies found rich, complex cultures, so the label was mostly dropped
Tribes today hold private property, so the old facts have changed
The Constitution of India forbids the word 'primitive' for tribes
Anthropologists still use the label today, but only for the smallest of the tribes

questions.q: In 2011, about 104 million tribal people belonged to 705 tribes. On average, that is roughly ___ lakh people per tribe (to one decimal place).

(a) A pupil says, 'Tribes treat a river as sacred because it gives them water.' What reason does the chapter give instead for treating natural elements as sacred? (b) Using your answer to (a), explain why the chapter says exchanges between folk, tribal and Hindu belief could happen 'so naturally'.
questions.a: (a) There is consciousness behind all of them: mountains, rivers, trees, plants, animals and some stones. (b) Folk, tribal and Hindu belief systems all hold this view of nature, and the chapter says such interactions took place so long and so naturally because the three share many similar concepts, so deities and rituals could pass between them easily.
s: Part (a): consciousness behind natural elements
Part (b): the shared concept made exchange natural, as the chapter says

questions.q: Farah writes: 'Tribes adopted ideas from Hinduism, but Hinduism also took ideas from tribal traditions.' Is her statement supported by the chapter? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. Tribes adopted Hindu deities long ago and have their own versions of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. In the other direction, Jagannath of Puri was, by tradition, originally a tribal deity, as were various forms of the mother-goddess. Andre Beteille adds that Hinduism, in its formative phase and throughout its evolution, has been influenced by tribal religions.
s: Verdict: supported
Tribal adoption of Hindu deities and epics
Hindu adoption of tribal deities such as Jagannath, or Beteille's view

questions.q: For a debate, Kavya must sum up Andre Beteille's view in one line. Which line is faithful to the quotation in the chapter?
questions.a: Beteille says that tribal religions being influenced by Hinduism is widely accepted, but it is equally true that Hinduism, in its formative phase and throughout its evolution, was influenced by tribal religions: influence ran both ways, all along. Each distractor keeps only one direction or limits it in time.
o: Influence ran both ways, from the start and all along
Hinduism influenced tribal religions, but not the reverse
Tribal religions shaped Hinduism only in its early phase
Castes and tribes kept apart until quite recent times

questions.q: A classmate says the word 'tribal' must refer to a small group of people in India. Show, using the chapter, that this cannot be true for India today.
questions.a: According to official figures, in 2011 India had 705 tribes spread over most States, with a population of about 104 million people. The chapter points out that this is more than the populations of Australia and the United Kingdom together. So India's tribal people are a very large population, not a small group.
s: 705 tribes spread over most States
About 104 million people in 2011
More than Australia and the UK together, so not a small group

questions.q: (a) Some tribes possess their own versions of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. Is this an example of Hinduism borrowing from tribes, or of tribes borrowing from Hinduism? (b) Using your answer to (a), what does the chapter's phrase 'from India's northeastern States, all the way to Tamil Nadu' add?
questions.a: (a) Tribes borrowing from Hinduism: the chapter says some tribes adopted Hindu deities long ago and possess their own versions of the two epics. (b) That this borrowing was not a local exception: it has been well documented across a very wide stretch of India, from the northeast to the far south.
s: Part (a): tribes borrowing from Hinduism
Part (b): the borrowing is documented across a wide part of India

questions.q: A researcher argues that worship of nature deities and belief in a supreme being cannot go together in one tribal tradition. Which deity from the chapter is the best single counter-example, because it is both?
questions.a: Donyipolo, worshipped by several tribes of Arunachal Pradesh, is a combined form of the Sun and the Moon who later rose to the higher status of a supreme god, so one deity is both. Singbonga is supreme but the chapter does not tie him to a natural element, Jagannath is not described as either, and the Toda peak deities are linked to nature but not called supreme.
o: Donyipolo, a Sun-and-Moon form who rose to be a supreme god
Singbonga, the creator worshipped by the Munda and Santhal
Jagannath of Puri, who by tradition was first a tribal deity of Odisha
The deities the Todas believe live on the Nilgiri peaks

questions.q: (a) A pupil's note reads: 'Munda and Santhal: Singbonga, a Sun-and-Moon god of Arunachal Pradesh.' Correct the note. (b) Using the corrected note, explain why a tribe that worships many deities of nature and also Singbonga is following a pattern the chapter also sees in Hinduism.
questions.a: (a) The Munda and Santhal tribals, among others, in eastern India, worship Singbonga, a supreme deity who created this whole world; the Sun-and-Moon god of Arunachal Pradesh is Donyipolo. (b) The chapter says that despite a multiplicity of deities, many tribal groups, as with Hinduism, have a concept of a higher divinity or supreme being, and Singbonga, creator of the whole world, is such a being.
s: Part (a): Singbonga, creator deity of the Munda and Santhal in eastern India
Part (b): many deities alongside a supreme being, as in Hinduism

questions.q: The chapter says the roots it first describes are 'well documented in many texts', yet it ends by saying folk and tribal beliefs 'also count among India's cultural roots'. Interpret why, giving three points.
questions.a: 1. Besides documented texts, India has rich oral traditions passed on through everyday practice, and folk and tribal traditions are among them. 2. There has been a constant, two-way interaction between these traditions and the leading schools of thought, with deities, concepts, legends and rituals exchanged in both directions. 3. The result of this long interaction has been mutual enrichment, so these beliefs helped shape the common trunk of Indian culture and are part of its roots.
s: Oral traditions are a source of culture besides texts
Constant two-way exchange with the leading schools of thought
The result was mutual enrichment, so they are roots too

questions.q: A letter in a newspaper says: 'Tribal belief systems are limited to spirits and minor deities, and they took everything from Hinduism while giving nothing back.' Write the key points of a reply. Your reply must make five points from the chapter, and it must say which part of the letter, if any, has some truth in it.
questions.a: 1. Not limited to minor deities: many tribal groups have a concept of a supreme being, such as Donyipolo (Arunachal Pradesh), Khandoba (central India) and Singbonga, creator of the whole world (Munda and Santhal). 2. Tribes regard mountains, rivers, trees and animals as sacred because there is consciousness behind them, a view shared with Hinduism. 3. Giving back: by tradition Jagannath of Puri and various forms of the mother-goddess were originally tribal deities. 4. Some truth: tribes did adopt Hindu deities and have their own versions of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, but that is only one direction. 5. Andre Beteille says it is equally true that Hinduism, in its formative phase and throughout its evolution, was influenced by tribal religions; the chapter calls the result mutual enrichment.
s: Supreme deities answer 'only minor deities', with an example
Sacred nature with consciousness behind it, shared with Hinduism
Tribal gifts to Hinduism: Jagannath or the mother-goddess
Concedes the true part: tribes adopted Hindu deities and epics
Beteille's two-way influence and mutual enrichment

questions.q: Compare the way 19th-century anthropologists described tribes with the way tribes are understood in this chapter, and analyse what changed. Use five points.
questions.a: 1. In the 19th century, anthropologists often described tribes as 'primitive' or 'inferior' to civilised people. 2. Deeper studies revealed rich and complex tribal cultures, and such biased judgments have been mostly abandoned. 3. Today anthropologists define a tribe neutrally: families or clans sharing common descent, culture and language, living as a close-knit community under a chief and holding no private property. 4. The Constitution uses respectful terms, 'tribes', 'tribal communities' and janjati; there are 705 tribes and about 104 million people (2011). 5. The chapter shows the complexity of tribal belief: sacred nature, supreme deities such as Singbonga, and two-way influence with Hinduism. What changed is that a label of inferiority gave way to a study of cultures on their own terms.
s: The 19th-century 'primitive' or 'inferior' label
Deeper studies and the abandoning of the bias
Today's anthropological definition
The Constitution's terms and the 2011 figures
The complexity of tribal belief, and a conclusion on what changed

questions.q:
A stall at a district cultural fair has four draft labels:
Label 1: 'Donyipolo: a combined form of the Sun and the Moon, worshipped by several tribes of Arunachal Pradesh, who later rose to be a supreme god'
Label 2: 'Singbonga: supreme deity who created this whole world, worshipped by the Munda and Santhal of central India'
Label 3: 'Khandoba: a god of parts of central India who rose to supreme status'
Label 4: 'The Todas of the Nilgiris: they point to their thirty sacred peaks during prayers'
(a) Which two labels are wrong?
(b) Rewrite Label 2.
(c) Rewrite Label 4.
(d) The stall has room for one more label, titled 'A gift from tribal traditions to Hinduism'. The two candidates are 'Jagannath of Puri, by tradition first a tribal deity' and 'Tribal versions of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana'. Which fits the title? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Labels 2 and 4. (b) 'Singbonga: supreme deity who created this whole world, worshipped by the Munda and Santhal tribals, among others, in eastern India.' (c) 'The Todas of the Nilgiris: over thirty peaks are homes of a god or goddess, so sacred that the Todas avoid pointing to them with a finger.' (d) The Jagannath label: by tradition Jagannath was originally a tribal deity who came to be worshipped at Puri, a gift from tribal tradition to Hinduism. The tribal epics show the opposite direction, tribes adopting from Hinduism.
s: Part (a): Labels 2 and 4
Part (b): Singbonga in eastern India, not central India
Part (c): the Todas avoid pointing at the sacred peaks
Part (d): Jagannath, because the epics flow the other way

questions.q:
For a project, a student team writes notes on four imaginary communities:
W: families share descent, culture and language; live as a close-knit community under a chief; land is held in common.
X: families share a language only; each family owns its own land; no chief.
Y: families share descent, culture and language; live close-knit under a chief; each family owns private plots.
Z: families share descent, culture and language; live close-knit in a forest; land is held in common; no chief, as elders decide together.
(a) Which community meets every part of the anthropologists' definition of a tribe given in the chapter?
(b) For Y and for Z, name the one feature of the definition each lacks.
(c) Would ancient India have called Z a 'tribe'? Justify your judgement from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) W. (b) Y holds private property, while a tribe holds no private property; Z has no chief, while the definition says the community lives under a chief. (c) No. Ancient India did not have a word for 'tribe'; a community like Z, living in a specific environment such as a forest, would simply have been seen as one of the janas.
s: Part (a): W
Part (b): Y has private property; Z has no chief
Part (c): no, ancient India had no word for tribe and would call Z a jana living in a forest
